### knudsenPump3d

This example is a standard showcase for the thermal creep effect at higher Knudsen numbers and rarefied ideal gases.
Thereby, two vessels with a temperature difference are connected by a pipe, whose walls conduct the temperature gradient between the two vessels.
This gradient leads to the acceleration of the gas particles that collide with the pipe wall.
Besides, the Knudsen slip effect plays a role, which, together with thermal creep, establishes a circulating flow in the pipe.

![Streamlines in the Knudsen pump.](/examples/microfluidics/knudsenPump3d/doc/fig/knudsenPump.png){#fig-knudsenPump width="70%"}

The thermal creep effect can be mathematically described as a wall velocity

$$
u_{tc} = \frac{3}{4} \frac{\mu R}{P} \Bigl(\frac{\partial T}{\partial s} \Bigr)_w.
$$

The resulting pressure difference caused by moving gas particles can be described with the following analytical expression:

$$
\triangle P = \Bigl( \frac{6 \mu^2 R_s}{R^2 P_m} \Bigr) \frac{\triangle T}{\bigl( 1 + 8 \frac{Kn}{1 + b Kn} \bigr)}
$$

The nitrogen by $Kn=0.05$ in the given Knudsen pump by 4 K temperature difference leads to the pressure development shown in @fig-knudsenPumpPlot.

![Pressure difference in the Knudsen pump. Numerical and analytical results.](/examples/microfluidics/knudsenPump3d/doc/fig/knudsenPumpPlot.png){#fig-knudsenPumpPlot width="60%"}
